title: Evidence-first alert triage
content: Start with the alert and its related context. Separate FACTS copied from telemetry, OBSERVATIONS derived from those facts, HYPOTHESES that include benign and malicious possibilities, and CONCLUSIONS supported by evidence. Compare the entity with a 7–30 day baseline when available. Severity and rule risk are prioritization signals, not proof. If evidence is insufficient, defer the conclusion and name the missing evidence.

title: Investigation evidence collection
topic: process network persistence and baseline context
content: Gather only the context needed to test the leading hypotheses: alert identity, event semantics, process and parent process, network activity, related events, file changes, user context, persistence, and host baseline. Use fields and indexes verified by tool output. A zero-row query is an evidence gap, not proof that the behavior did not occur. Preserve the source and time window of each observation.

title: IOC verification and correlation
content: Extract an IOC verbatim from observed telemetry, correlate it with related events, and record where it appeared: process, network, file, registry, or alert field. Mark an indicator VERIFIED only when current evidence confirms it; otherwise mark it UNVERIFIED. An IOC value or reputation hit alone does not establish incident scope or maliciousness.

title: Evidence-based risk and severity assessment
content: Use unknown when suspicious activity lacks corroborating evidence or a baseline. Benign requires positive evidence of legitimacy and expected context. Malicious requires a strong indicator such as confirmed command-and-control, persistence, credential theft, lateral movement, defense evasion, a known malware match, or exfiltration. Alert severity and rule names are not evidence by themselves.

title: False-positive reasoning for suspicious behavior
topic: legitimate administration testing and software context
content: Check legitimate enterprise management, security software, software protection, large application frameworks, and designated testing before calling behavior malicious. Useful benign context includes a known parent process, approved vendor signature, maintenance window, expected software installation, or a test harness. A suspicious PowerShell execution, temporary path, unsigned file, or network connection alone should remain unknown until corroborated.

title: Baseline-driven threat hunting
content: Hunt by comparing current activity with historical behavior for the same host, user, process, action, or destination. Rare or new behavior is a prioritization signal that needs corroboration, not a verdict. Keep the time range, entity, query purpose, and returned fields explicit so another analyst can reproduce the observation.

title: Read-only incident response next actions
topic: evidence gaps escalation and containment recommendations
source: Local Elastic security-case-management and alert-triage guidance
content: After analysis, summarize facts, observations, hypotheses, conclusion status, evidence gaps, and recommended next actions. Keep containment or remediation as a recommendation unless an authorized workflow explicitly permits it. Do not disable accounts, block indicators, delete data, change configuration, acknowledge alerts, or modify cases from SOC RAG guidance alone. If evidence is missing, say: Not available from current evidence.

title: Detection tuning with scoped validation
topic: rule logic false-positive tuning and simulation
content: Before tuning a detection, identify the exact rule and understand its logic. Measure host and user spread, inspect dominant patterns, perform the required entity cross-check, and simulate the proposed exclusion before applying it. Scope exceptions to the rule and prefer precise full-path or entity conditions. When uncertain, do not broaden an exception.

title: Authentication alert investigation
topic: login failures accounts and source behavior
source: Local Splunk splunk-security-alert-triage and splunk-authentication SKILL.md
content: For an authentication alert, verify the alert or notable first, then examine failed and successful outcomes, source behavior, target account behavior, timing, and a historical baseline. Do not infer brute force from one failure or from a severity label. Look for repeated attempts, concentration on accounts or sources, and corroborating activity while preserving the exact fields returned by the provider.

title: Kerberoasting (T1558.003)
topic: credential access and service ticket abuse
content: MITRE ATT&CK describes Kerberoasting as abuse of Kerberos service tickets, including obtaining a ticket-granting service ticket for a service account and attempting offline password recovery. Investigate the requesting principal, targeted service accounts and SPNs, ticket request timing and volume, encryption types when available, and corroborating account or host activity. The technique label is guidance; map it as observed only when alert fields or telemetry support it.

title: PowerShell (T1059.001)
content: MITRE ATT&CK classifies adversary use of PowerShell under Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell. For a suspicious execution alert, collect the exact command line, script or encoded content when available, parent and child process context, user, host, signer, download or network activity, persistence, and baseline. PowerShell execution alone is not proof of maliciousness; compare with approved administration and software deployment activity.

title: Brute Force (T1110)
content: MITRE ATT&CK maps repeated credential guessing behavior to Brute Force (T1110). Test the hypothesis against counts and timing of failed and successful authentication, source and destination spread, targeted account patterns, lockouts, geographic or network context, and a known-good baseline. Distinguish password spraying, credential stuffing, and single-account guessing only when evidence supports the subtype.

title: Web Protocols (T1071.001)
content: MITRE ATT&CK maps adversary use of HTTP or HTTPS for application-layer communication to Web Protocols (T1071.001). A suspicious network connection needs process ownership, destination, DNS or domain context, timing, response or byte behavior, certificate or reputation evidence when available, and host baseline. A network connection alone is not proof of command and control.
